concept_name: Uniform Circular Motion — Circling Needs a Constant Inward Force
source_book: NCERT Class 11 Physics Ch.4 §4.11 (uniform circular motion) + Ch.5 §5.9 (Laws of Motion — circular-motion dynamics) — table-of-contents scope only, teaching authored from first principles. The atomic concept: a body moving in a circle at constant speed is not in equilibrium — it needs a net force pointing at the centre at every instant, and on this apparatus that force is the string's tension (or the tension's horizontal component once gravity joins) — never a new kind of force, and never an outward one. Does NOT cover the kinematic derivation a = v squared over r (that belongs to centripetal_acceleration_kinematic, not yet shipped), a car on a level or banked road (that belongs to circular_motion_banking and related atomics, deliberately out), non-uniform vertical circular motion (taught after work-energy), centrifugal force as a rotating-frame tool (this concept shows only that no outward force exists in the ground frame), angular kinematics theta/omega/alpha as a system, or period and frequency as a formal topic. Built on the force_rig field_3d engine (docs/loop_runs/lom_g/_engine/force_rig_json_contract.md), branch B `whirl`, pure configuration, zero renderer edits. DC Pandey and NCERT tables of contents consulted for chapter placement only; no teaching sequence, example problem, figure or explanation phrasing imported.

real_world_anchor.primary: A ball whirled on a string, and the moment you let go. Every student has whirled something on a string or swung a bag in a circle, and every student has the body-memory that it flies outward when released — which is exactly wrong, and exactly what this concept settles. The anchor IS the apparatus: no translation gap between the hook and the sim.
real_world_anchor.secondary: A spin dryer. A washing machine's spin cycle dries clothes because the drum turns and the water does NOT get flung outward — at each hole, water that loses its inward hold simply keeps going straight along the tangent it had, and leaves through the wall. A household machine on every syllabus's territory, no country, brand or place named.

theta.name: cone half-angle from the vertical — SOLVED, never authored

r.name: radius of the circle the ball sweeps

W.name: weight of the ball (conical states only)

omega_min.name: smallest spin rate for which a cone exists

T_N.formula: m * omega^2 * L — tension in the string, N; 13.50 N at the STATE_1/STATE_2 default geometry, up to 57.66 N at STATE_5's ramp end.

theta_deg_display.formula: degrees(acos(clamp(g/(omega^2 L),0,1))) — cone half-angle from the vertical, deg; not defined on the flat geometry (STATE_1-3), 32.0 deg to 75.2 deg across the conical guided states.

v_ms.formula: omega * r — tangential speed, m/s; 3.00 m/s at STATE_1's default, held at 1.80 m/s through STATE_3's cut.

omega_min_display.formula: sqrt(g / L) — smallest spin rate for which a cone exists, rad/s; 3.13 rad/s at L = 1.00 m (STATE_6's clamp boundary).

constraints: the tension always points from the ball toward the anchor, solved by the engine, never authored
the velocity is always tangent to the circle the ball is sweeping, at every instant
no outward force exists anywhere, at any time — the largest outward radial component of any drawn arrow, measured over a full revolution, is 0.000
theta is SOLVED from omega and L via cos theta = g / (omega^2 L); it is never authored, and the engine clamps omega to sqrt(g/L) below which no conical solution exists (the bob hangs, theta = 0)

on the flat plane the normal force exactly cancels gravity, so the string tension is the ONLY horizontal force on the ball; T = m omega^2 L holds on every geometry (r = L on flat, r = L sin theta on the cone)
the post-cut straight line is the output of deleting the string constraint from the integrator; it is never a scripted animation

aha_moment.statement: Cut the string: the ball goes straight, tangent — no outward force ever existed.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: The straight trail leaves the dim ghost circle; v holds 1.80 m/s before and after the cut, and T drops to 0 N.

exit_pills.foundational_to_conical: What if the ball also hangs under gravity? →

scene_composition.text: Tension pulls inward, always
ω = 3.00 rad/s, T = 13.5 N — string pulls ball toward centre
velocity direction turns continuously; its size stays 3.00 m/s

tts_sentences.text_en: The ball circles at a steady speed, but its direction changes every instant, so the velocity is not constant.
The string pulls the ball toward the centre continuously, a nonzero force; balanced forces add to zero, unlike here.

scene_composition.text: Faster spin, larger tension
ω grows 3.00 → 6.00 rad/s; T grows 13.5 → 54.0 N
T grows with ω squared, not with ω itself

tts_sentences.text_en: As the spin rate doubles, the tension needed to hold the ball on its circle does not just double — it grows with the square of the spin rate.
Watch the string's pull grow far faster than the speed does.

scene_composition.text: Cut: straight along tangent
before the cut: v = 1.80 m/s, T = 12.96 N
after the cut: v still 1.80 m/s, T = 0 N — straight trail, no outward push

tts_sentences.text_en: The ball keeps circling steadily, held on its circle only by the string's inward pull.
No force ever pushes the ball outward — just watch what happens when the string is cut.
It moves straight, tangent, at the same speed.

misconception_watch.belief: A whirled object is flung outward — cut the string and it flies away from the centre along the radius.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The straight tangent trail departs alongside the dim abandoned ghost circle; v reads 1.80 m/s both before and after the cut, and T drops to 0 N — no outward force is ever drawn.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Nothing throws the ball outward — with the pull gone it keeps its velocity, straight along the tangent.

STATE_4.title: Tension's Two Components
STATE_4.motion_archetype: orbit-steady (declared contrast pair with STATE_1 — the flat plane is gone; the string tilts to θ = 52.2° and one tension carries two jobs at once)

scene_composition.text: Tension splits: vertical and inward
T = 24.0 N, θ = 52.2° — vertical part balances mg = 14.7 N
horizontal part of the same tension is the net inward force ΣF

tts_sentences.text_en: Now gravity acts on the ball: the string tilts, and the ball hangs at an angle while it circles.
The one tension now has two components.
Its vertical component balances the pull of gravity on the ball; its horizontal component points at the centre — the net inward force that keeps the ball circling.

scene_composition.text: Faster spin opens the cone
ω grows 3.40 → 6.20 rad/s; θ opens 32.0° → 75.2°
T climbs 17.3 → 57.7 N; the string stops short of horizontal

tts_sentences.text_en: Spin the ball faster, and the cone angle is not something we choose — it is solved by the physics.
As the spin rate climbs, the string swings up, closer to horizontal, and the tension climbs sharply.
But it never quite reaches horizontal, no matter how fast the ball spins.

misconception_watch.belief: Spin fast enough and the string will rise to horizontal, with the bob level with the pivot.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: θ reaches 75.2° at ω = 6.20 rad/s — near the top of this rig's range — and stops there; cos θ = g/(ω²L) never reaches zero at any real spin rate.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Horizontal needs cos θ = 0, and g/(ω²L) is never zero — the string gets close, never level.

STATE_6.title: Below Minimum Spin, No Cone
STATE_6.motion_archetype: cone-collapse (declared reversal pair with STATE_5 — ramp DOWN through ω_min = 3.13 rad/s; the cone closes to θ = 0 and the revolution ends)

scene_composition.text: Too slow: no cone
ω falls 4.50 → 2.60 rad/s; θ closes 61.1° → 0°
below ω_min = 3.13 rad/s the guide ring vanishes and the ball hangs

tts_sentences.text_en: Slow the spin, and the cone shrinks toward zero.
Cosine cannot exceed one, so a smallest spin rate exists below which no cone can form.
The string hangs straight down, and the ball stops circling.

scene_composition.text: Change spin, length, mass
spin rate, string length and mass are all live sliders
drive ω below the minimum and watch the honest clamp

tts_sentences.text_en: Change the spin rate, the string length, or the mass, and watch how the cone and the tension respond.

regeneration_variants.label: A Spin Dryer Draining Water From Clothes
regeneration_variants.physical_world: A washing machine's spin cycle turns a drum full of wet clothes at high speed; water leaves through holes in the drum wall.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: Identical circular-motion physics: water that loses its inward hold at a hole simply continues straight along the tangent it had at that instant — it is never flung outward, it is left behind by the turning drum.
regeneration_variants.scene_hint: Same whirl fixture — only the labelled world changes from a ball on a string to a drop of water at the drum wall.

regeneration_variants.label: A Bag Or Bucket Swung In A Circle
regeneration_variants.physical_world: A bag, a bucket of water, or a ball on a rope is swung around in a circle by hand — a universal childhood experiment.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: Identical tension-provides-centripetal-force physics: the hand's grip, through the rope, supplies the same inward pull the string supplies here; let go, and the object leaves straight along the tangent, exactly as the whirl rig shows.
regeneration_variants.scene_hint: Same whirl fixture — only the labelled world changes from a lab string-and-ball to a hand-swung bag or bucket.

assessment.mastery_definition: A student has mastered uniform circular motion when they can (1) state that a body circling at constant SPEED still needs a net force pointing at the centre, because its velocity's DIRECTION is always changing; (2) apply T = m ω² r and explain that tension grows with the SQUARE of the spin rate, not with the spin rate itself; (3) predict that a released whirled body moves straight along the tangent at unchanged speed, and explain why no outward force ever existed; (4) resolve a conical pendulum's tension into a vertical component that balances weight and a horizontal component that is the net inward force, and state that T > mg always on a real cone; (5) use the solved relation cos θ = g/(ω²L) to explain that the cone opens as spin rises but never reaches horizontal; (6) state the existence condition ω ≥ √(g/L) for a conical pendulum, and describe what happens below it.

questions.stem: A ball moves in a circle at a constant SPEED. Is there a net force acting on it, and if so, which way does it point?

options.A: Yes — a net force points toward the centre at every instant, because the velocity's DIRECTION keeps changing even though its size does not
options.B: No — since the speed is constant, the net force on the ball must be zero
options.C: Yes, but it points along the direction of motion, keeping the ball moving forward
options.D: Yes, but it points away from the centre, balancing the ball's tendency to fly outward

distractor_misconceptions.B: the core misconception this state exists to break — confuses constant SPEED with constant VELOCITY; the direction changes every instant, so the net force is not zero
distractor_misconceptions.C: confuses the force that would speed the ball up with the one that actually acts — an along-motion force would change the SPEED, which stays constant here
distractor_misconceptions.D: invents an outward force with no source; nothing pulls or pushes the ball away from the centre — only the inward tension acts

questions.tested_idea: Constant-speed circling still needs a net inward force, because the velocity's direction is always changing.
questions.parallel_form_stem: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle at unchanging speed. State whether any net force acts on it and, if so, its direction.

questions.stem: A ball on a string needs tension T to hold it in a circle of radius r at spin rate ω. If the spin rate is doubled (radius unchanged), what happens to the tension?

options.A: It becomes four times as large, since T = m ω² r and ω is squared
options.B: It becomes twice as large, since tension should scale the same way as spin rate
options.C: It stays the same, since the string length and mass have not changed
options.D: It becomes half as large, since the ball now completes the circle in less time

distractor_misconceptions.B: assumes a direct proportionality that the formula does not have — T depends on ω SQUARED, not ω itself
distractor_misconceptions.C: misses that ω is one of the three quantities T depends on: T = m ω² r changes whenever ω changes, even with m and r fixed
distractor_misconceptions.D: confuses a shorter period with a smaller force — a shorter period comes WITH a larger ω, which INCREASES the tension needed, not decreases it

questions.tested_idea: Doubling the spin rate quadruples the needed tension, since T = m ω² r.
questions.parallel_form_stem: A ball on a string requires 20 N of tension to circle at a given spin rate. If the spin rate is doubled, find the new tension.

questions.stem: A ball is whirled in a horizontal circle on a string. The string is cut. Which way does the ball move immediately afterward, and at what speed?

options.A: Straight along the tangent to the circle at that instant, at the SAME speed it had the moment before
options.B: Straight outward along the radius, away from the centre, speeding up as it goes
options.C: Straight along the tangent, but slower than before, since the inward pull was helping it move
options.D: It keeps moving in the same circle for a moment, then gradually straightens out

distractor_misconceptions.B: the exact belief this state exists to break — no outward force exists at any point before or after the cut; the ball's velocity was always tangential, never radial
distractor_misconceptions.C: assumes the tension was contributing to the SPEED, but tension always acted perpendicular to the velocity, so it never did work on the ball; removing it changes nothing about the speed
distractor_misconceptions.D: invents a gradual transition with no physical cause — the constraint disappears the instant the string is cut, and the ball's motion follows its existing velocity from that instant

questions.tested_idea: A released ball moves along the tangent at unchanged speed — there is no outward force.
questions.parallel_form_stem: A ball whirled on a string breaks free mid-circle. Describe its path and speed in the instant right after.

questions.stem: A ball hangs from a string and swings in a horizontal circle, with the string tilted at angle θ from the vertical (a conical pendulum). How does the string's tension compare to the ball's weight mg?

options.A: T = mg / cos θ, which is always LARGER than mg, since cos θ is less than 1 for any real cone
options.B: T = mg exactly, the same as if the ball were just hanging still
options.C: T = mg cos θ, which is always SMALLER than mg
options.D: T depends only on the spin rate, and has no fixed relationship to mg

distractor_misconceptions.B: ignores that the string is TILTED — only the string's VERTICAL component (T cos θ) balances mg, so T itself must be larger than mg to supply that component
distractor_misconceptions.C: inverts the relationship — T cos θ = mg means T = mg / cos θ, not T = mg cos θ
distractor_misconceptions.D: misses that the vertical balance T cos θ = mg fixes a relationship between T and mg at any angle, even though θ itself is set by the spin rate

questions.tested_idea: On the cone, T cos θ = mg, so T > mg always.
questions.parallel_form_stem: A conical pendulum's string makes a 40° angle with the vertical. State whether its tension is larger, smaller, or equal to the bob's weight, and why.

questions.stem: In a conical pendulum, the string's angle from the vertical is given by cos θ = g / (ω² L). As the spin rate ω is increased without limit, what happens to θ?

options.A: θ keeps increasing toward 90°, but never reaches it — reaching horizontal would need an infinitely large ω
options.B: θ increases and reaches exactly 90° once ω is large enough
options.C: θ stays fixed once ω passes a certain value, since the string cannot open any further
options.D: θ increases past 90°, so the ball swings above the level of the pivot

distractor_misconceptions.B: the exact belief this state exists to break — cos θ = g/(ω²L) is zero only in the limit ω → ∞, never at any finite spin rate
distractor_misconceptions.C: invents a physical stop with no basis — the formula keeps giving a smaller cos θ, and so a larger θ, for every larger ω, with no ceiling short of 90°
distractor_misconceptions.D: assumes θ can exceed the geometric limit of a hanging string; a string held from above cannot swing the bob above the pivot's level

questions.tested_idea: cos θ = g/(ω²L); the string never reaches horizontal at any finite spin rate.
questions.parallel_form_stem: A conical pendulum's spin rate is increased again and again. Explain what happens to the string's angle, and whether it can ever become exactly horizontal.

questions.stem: A conical pendulum's angle is set by cos θ = g / (ω² L). What happens if the spin rate ω is reduced below √(g / L)?

options.A: No conical motion is possible below that spin rate — cos θ would have to exceed 1, so the string simply hangs straight down
options.B: The cone still forms, just at a very small angle close to 0°
options.C: The ball swings in a circle below the horizontal, on the far side of vertical
options.D: Any spin rate, however small, produces some cone angle greater than zero

distractor_misconceptions.B: the exact belief this state exists to break — below ω = √(g/L), cos θ = g/(ω²L) EXCEEDS 1, which has no solution; there is no small positive angle left, the cone collapses entirely to θ = 0
distractor_misconceptions.C: invents a geometry the string cannot produce — a string held from a fixed point above can only hang at or below that point, never form a cone on the far side of vertical
distractor_misconceptions.D: misses the existence boundary entirely — below the minimum spin rate the formula gives no valid angle, so the bob simply hangs, it does not keep some tiny cone

questions.tested_idea: Conical motion exists only for ω ≥ √(g/L); below it the bob hangs.
questions.parallel_form_stem: A conical pendulum's spin rate is slowed down more and more. State the exact condition at which the cone disappears, and what the bob does below that spin rate.

entries.syllabus_unit: Laws of Motion — dynamics of circular motion; conical pendulum
Circular motion — angular speed, centripetal force

STATE_1.label: Circling at constant speed still needs a continuous inward pull
STATE_1.caption: Tension pulls inward, always

STATE_2.label: The inward pull grows with the SQUARE of the spin rate: T = m ω² r
STATE_2.caption: Faster spin, larger tension

STATE_3.label: Cut the string: the ball departs straight, tangent, at unchanged speed — no outward force exists
STATE_3.caption: Cut: straight along tangent

STATE_4.label: With gravity, one tension has two components — vertical balances weight, horizontal is the inward force
STATE_4.caption: Tension splits: vertical and inward

STATE_5.label: The cone angle is solved: cos θ = g/(ω²L); faster spin opens it, never to horizontal
STATE_5.caption: Faster spin opens the cone

STATE_6.label: Below ω = √(g/L) there is no cone — the bob simply hangs
STATE_6.caption: Too slow: no cone

STATE_7.label: Explore: spin, length and mass all live; the ω minimum clamp is honest at the slider
STATE_7.caption: Change spin, length, mass
